court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Concerns whether a life-estate lease of agricultural land violates the twelve-year constitutional limit on agricultural leases; no lodging, boarding, or short-term dwelling occupancy involved.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Concerns police stationing an officer inside a restaurant/gambling house to inspect for gambling; no lodging or boarding-house letting at issue.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Ordinary commercial landlord-tenant holding-over dispute involving a business tenant (an incorporated railway-equipment concern); no lodging or boarding letting.

cite: People ex rel. Murphy v. Lockwood, 10 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 304
notes: Summary-proceedings dispute over whether a conventional landlord-tenant relation existed between an owner's agent and a woman occupying the house; no rent/board for lodging at issue, occupancy claimed by right of inheritance, not compensated short-term letting.

cite: McCafferty v. Decker, 10 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 604
notes: Action for money had and received arising from a railroad contractor's deduction of boarding-house debts from laborers' wages; boarding houses mentioned only incidentally to a wage-deduction custom, not the legality or regulation of letting rooms.

cite: O'Rourke v. People, 10 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 225
notes: Concerns excise-license classes for selling strong liquors and ale/beer (inn/tavern/hotel keepers vs. other licensees); a liquor-licensing dispute, not lodging/boarding regulation.

cite: Shallies v. Wilcox, 9 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 419
holding_summary: A lease of a store for $300/year included a covenant by the lessor-householder to board the tenant at his own house during the lease term; when the lessor refused to continue boarding him, the court held the tenant entitled to recoup the value of the board against the rent owed.

quotes.text: the said Nelson Shallies further agrees, in consideration of the above covenants and agreements, to board the said Eugene W. Wilcox during said term, at his house in Arcade.
The defendant clearly had a right of recoupment and counter-claim, to the extent of the value of his board from the time in the said half year that the plaintiff Shallies had refused to board him.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The keeper of a public house for the lodging of travelers sought to enjoin police from stationing officers outside his house and warning strangers to be careful before entering; the court refused the injunction, holding that police protection of strangers and emigrants justified such warnings where guests had repeatedly been subjected to exorbitant and illegal charges.

quotes.text: The plaintiff in this case keeps a public house on Hubert street, for the entertainment and lodging of travelers.

I am of opinion that such protection would sustain a warning “to take care,” or “to be careful,” to a person, a stranger, about to enter a public house in which guests had been repeatedly subjected to extortionate, exorbitant and illegal charges, and of which notice had been brought to the police authorities.

cite: Evers v. People, 10 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 716
notes: Criminal appeal on self-defense evidentiary rulings; the prisoner's mention of holding a license for a sailors' boarding house is a passing biographical detail, not a holding about lodging/boarding legality.

cite: People ex rel. Ward v. Kelsey, 14 Abb. Pr. 372
notes: Concerns whether a reclaimed wharf/pier is a 'tenement' subject to summary landlord-tenant proceedings; a commercial pier lease, not residential lodging or boarding.

cite: People ex rel. Mitchell v. Simpson, 14 Abb. Pr. 457
notes: Purely procedural: sufficiency of an affidavit to establish a landlord-tenant relation for summary dispossession proceedings between a grantor and grantee; no lodging/boarding practice involved.

cite: Toub v. Schmidt, 67 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 409
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Defines the innkeeper/guest relationship for purposes of an innkeeper's tort/bailment liability for lost goods (a peddler who neither engaged a room nor ate/drank was held not a 'guest'); this is a liability-scope holding, not one bearing on the legality or regulation of letting/lodging arrangements, so treated as off-topic despite touching innkeeping doctrine.

cite: Purdy v. Bennett, 75 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 227
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Procedural ejectment-judgment-vacatur dispute (Code of Civil Procedure section 1536); a five-year agricultural-land lease is mentioned only as background, no lodging/boarding practice at issue.

cite: Higgins v. Hallock, 67 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 125
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: An executor who promised to see a boarding-house keeper paid for taking in a deceased man's orphaned children was held individually and unconditionally liable for the value of their board, the boarding-house keeper's performance being sufficient consideration for the promise.

quotes.text: directed the plaintiff, who kept a boarding-house, to take and keep them and he would see her paid.

Held, that the statement of Hallock must be deemed an unconditional promise to pay for the support of the children, and that performance by the boardinghouse keeper furnished a legal consideration in support thereof.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Concerns whether a sheriff who remained in commercial premises after a levy became liable as a tenant for use and occupation; a commercial floor-space dispute, not lodging/boarding.

cite: Senecal v. Thousand Island Steamboat Co., 86 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 574
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Wrongful-death/negligence action over a steamboat collision; testimony that a witness's father-in-law 'kept a boarding house and a bar' is a passing biographical detail on cross-examination, not a holding on lodging/boarding legality.
Same case as People v. Evers, 10 N.Y. Sup. Ct. 716 (self-defense/assault appeal); the 'sailors' boarding-house' license is a passing biographical detail, not a holding on lodging/boarding legality.

cite: Hine v. New York Elevated Railroad, 7 N.Y.S. 464
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Concerns an abutting owner's easements of light, air, and access against an elevated railroad, and the applicability of Dutch colonial law versus the common law to Bowery street title; no lodging or boarding-house letting at issue.
